By The New Yorker August 26, 2026
The Best Books of 2026 So Far
All Books
Nonfiction
Fiction & Poetry
All Them Dogs
by Djamel White ( Riverhead )
Fiction
“I was Wardy. Tony bleeding Ward. Lethal weapon forged in 1997,” the protagonist of this bold début novel proclaims. The statement is mainly a reminder to himself, as he returns home to Dublin after five long years on the run. Tony had to flee after killing a member of a rival gang; now he has joined the ranks of another outfit, notionally in search of money and protection, but ultimately out of a longing to have “someone else do the thinking.” As Tony strains to navigate brewing street wars, the most intimidating battles he faces are still internal—between expectation and desire, between who he is and who he might want to be.

American Sophistication
by Ross Posnock ( Princeton )
Nonfiction
“This is how the ‘sophisticated’ talk about sophistication: they don’t.” So begins this new study of the American sense of ‘cool,’ before then embarking on an encyclopedic review of the ideal from pre-Revolutionary times to the postmodern age. Breathtakingly large in scope and purpose, and almost flamboyantly digressive and parenthetical, it’s sure to entertain and provoke. Ultimately, Posnock argues the high-water mark of American sophistication was in the nineteen-fifties, and offers a grand unified theory of the subject—one that identifies a particularly American spin on older European ideals and uncovers the values baked into its casual style.

Sex and Dissent
by Meaghan Beatley ( Penguin )
Nonfiction
This vividly reported book centers on recent feminist movements in Argentina, Chile, Mexico, and Spain. Beatley, a journalist, profiles women protesting abortion restrictions, sexual assault, and femicide—an act that, she writes, lies “atop layers of normalized and socially sanctioned abuse.” While documenting acts of resistance, she examines the way that these feminists’ cultural contexts inflect their organizing. As she points out, many were influenced by struggles against military dictatorships of the twentieth century; some are the children of disappeared dissidents. “What sets Latin America apart is not violence itself but the clarity with which women understand its roots,” she writes.

The Disappearers
by Marlon James ( Riverhead )
Fiction
This novel, James’s sixth, follows a group of gay men in Jamaica who seek love, connection, and restitution after a bloody homophobic attack. The explosion of malice effaces the men in different ways, and the book traces the mechanisms of their vanishing, examining how a person’s life can be compressed into smaller and smaller spaces. James blurs his actors together in slightly eerie ways, as if to show how suffering flattens and homogenizes its victims. But the permeability of James’s protagonists also suggests the liberating malleability of social roles. “The Disappearers” uses the tricks of fiction to pull off something extremely difficult: giving full weight to tragedy and injustice without implying that some lives are over before they’ve begun.

Solstice
by Carol Gilligan ( Random House )
Fiction
This tender novel of intimacy and its risks begins in Boston in 1969, as Eve, a dancer, commences an affair with a colleague—an indiscretion that spurs her husband, a journalist named Gabe, to cheat, too. Under the influence of their era’s changing sexual mores, they soon reconcile. But then, in the eighties, Gabe returns from a reporting trip to the Middle East having taken up with a much younger woman. By this time, the couple share decades of history, along with three children. Gilligan’s portrait of their relationship is a study of how time binds people together. “There was a membrane now stretching between them,” she writes, “encompassing the two of them and enclosing them, fragile and yet impermeable.”

Endless Endings
by Ricard Solé , translated from the Spanish by Eduardo Aparicio ( Princeton )
Nonfiction
A single cell serves as the starting point for this lyrical exploration of death. From a consideration of apoptosis—the orderly elimination of damaged or unnecessary cells—Solé moves on to failing machines, eroded memories, vanished languages, brittle digital archives, and more. His overarching idea is that organisms, minds, technologies, and cultures survive by sustaining flows of matter, energy, or information; their final deaths occur not when a single constituent part disappears but when the processes holding the larger system together falter. Solé reveals a paradox: death is not merely life’s opposite but also one of its organizing forces, a constant cycle of removal and renewal through which complex systems are preserved.

The Black Shield
by Wilbert L. Cooper ( Farrar, Straus & Giroux )
Nonfiction
In this multilayered work, a journalist examines a Black police organization, known as the Black Shield, that emerged in Cleveland in the nineteen-forties, alongside his own parents’ membership in it. Cooper assesses the notion that Black communities are “safer and served better” when the police who surveil and discipline them are Black, too. In theory, he writes, the Black Shield offers opportunity for young people living in the economically distressed community where it is based, but he concludes that the group is less focussed on justice than on “getting the same lack of accountability that White officers enjoyed.” His ultimate indictment is nuanced, and has shades of appreciation—for his parents, and for the badge that “shielded my family.”

Supremacy
by Nikolas Bowie Daphna Renan ( Norton )
Nonfiction
This formidable, sharply argued history of the Supreme Court tracks the ascendance of “judicial supremacy” over two hundred years, focussing on how the Court seized the power to strike down acts of Congress. Its power to invalidate state and local laws is a double-edged sword, but its ability to overrule a coequal branch, the authors maintain, has reliably served regressive ends. By tracing the origins of this self-conferred authority, the Harvard Law School professors make the provocative case that the Supreme Court needs to be cut down to size, and that Congress should reclaim its rightful authority.

I Was Bonnie & Clyde
by Laura Kasischke ( Copper Canyon )
Poetry
The wily, beguiling poems in this collection probe selves and stories as sites of rupture and refraction. The book’s eponymous poem, for instance, begins, “You were Friday & Death. / I was Jekyll & Hyde. / You were my mother. / I Alive.” Throughout, Kasischke’s images ricochet off one another—suggesting narrative while resisting its confines, evoking stereotypical ideas and expectations of Western womanhood only to upend them. In a voice at once biting and contemplative, eerie and funny, Kasischke crafts poems in which nothing is ever stable or resolved. There is only “The confusion of the past / as fireproof as ash. // The follies of the future / as bulletproof as water.”

The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State
by Jill Lepore ( Liveright )
Nonfiction
In this wide-ranging history, Lepore traces the ideas and technologies that have transformed political life, from census-taking and technocracy to social media and A.I. Our growing reliance on machines to predict and shape human behavior, Lepore argues, threatens democratic self-government and augurs a deeper estrangement from the natural world. The book grew out of a piece that ran in the magazine in 2024.

The Anniversary
by Andrea Bajani , translated from the Italian by Geoffrey Brock ( Other Press )
Fiction
“Ten years ago, I saw my parents for the last time,” proclaims the narrator—an unnamed man—of this unsparing novel. “I’ve erected an impregnable wall and put an ocean between us. They’ve been the best ten years of my life.” He, in commemoration of the decade-long estrangement from his mother and father, reflects on their lives and on his upbringing. The book, which was excerpted in the magazine, challenges readers to reconsider what they owe their families, particularly in light of what they owe themselves.

A Tender Age
by Chang-rae Lee ( Riverhead )
Fiction
In the spring of 1976, Jeon-Gi, the narrator of Lee’s seventh novel, is on the cusp of turning eleven. He’s growing up at a time when childhood is a free-range affair, and he spends hours roaming outside with a gang of other kids, figuring out how to negotiate both a fractured friendship and the demands of a neighborhood bully. His parents, recent Korean immigrants, know little of his troubles, and are shocked when violence erupts and fifth grade for Jeon-Gi comes to an abrupt halt. A summer camp, organized by a Korean church, gives him an opportunity to forge new friendships, but, once again, everything changes in an instant. Years later, Jeon-Gi is still haunted by his actions—and the lingering mystery of his intentions. In this immersive and thought-provoking novel, which was excerpted in the magazine, the reader may feel more sympathy for Jeon-Gi than he does for himself.

The Yahoo Boys
by Carlos Barragán ( Farrar, Straus & Giroux )
Nonfiction
In 2022, the author of this engrossing investigation travelled to Lagos, Nigeria, to find the person who, years earlier, ensnared his mother in an online romance scam. What he discovered was a place primed by its history and its poverty for the emergence of youths, known as Yahoo Boys, dedicated to conning Western marks using false identities, fake naked pictures, and flattery. In Barragán’s account, Nigerian public discourse casts the Yahoo life style—fuelled by drugs and extravagant spending—as a double-edged sword, both a stain on the country’s reputation and a powerful economic engine. As the book follows four Yahoos, it assembles a story of loneliness in the digital age—a loneliness that deforms scammer and scammed alike.

A Scandal in Königsberg
by Christopher Clark ( Penguin Press )
Nonfiction
This fine and detailed book reconstructs a sex scandal that erupted in the eighteen-thirties in the Prussian city of Königsberg, which quickly captured public attention across the kingdom and beyond. After an earnest clergyman, with long shiny curls parted “like a lady,” attracted a cluster of devoted women followers, it didn’t take long for townspeople to suspect the charismatic cleric of arousing more than religious zealotry. Clark highlights the now familiar patterns of public inquisition from this odd historical case study, with rumors elevated into accusations and lives destroyed before anyone has established what has actually happened. As the book’s foreword cautions: “Resemblances to present-day persons and situations, though not intended, cannot be ruled out.”

Unsayable
by Michael Cunningham ( Random House )
Nonfiction
When this warm memoir begins, the author, a celebrated novelist, observes that the world is “sufficient unto itself. It neither knows nor cares if anyone writes about it.” Why write, then? In the pages that follow, Cunningham remembers his upbringing in middle-class suburban California, his gradual awareness of his gayness, his time as a countercultural student at Stanford, and his stints working as a hustler and a bartender, all the while elaborating writing’s many purposes—and offering guidance on how to do it well. It’s a way to entertain, to turn “ephemera into objects,” to “render and recognize everything and everyone.”

A Violent Masterpiece
by Jordan Harper ( Mulholland )
Fiction
Harper’s crime novel alternates between the perspectives of three characters. Kara Delgado works as a fixer at L.A.’s premier concierge service, catering to the outré tastes and perversions of the city’s élite. Doug Gibson is a pugilistic criminal-defense lawyer, the kind with ads on bus-stop benches. Jake Deal, formerly employed to dig up secrets for a gossip website, now works for himself as a live-streamer; he drives through the city, using a police scanner to track down scenes of chaos and carnage, feeding his viewers’ appetite for vérité gore. What is the line, Harper seems to ask, between documenting the horrors of the world and profiting from them, packaging them for an audience safe at home?

Presence
by Erin Maglaque ( Astra )
Nonfiction
This “hidden history of the female body” reveals the ways that natural processes, such as giving birth, have been shaped by changing medical beliefs and social arrangements. Drawing on physicians’ casebooks, midwifery manuals, household recipe collections, court testimonies, private letters, and more, Maglaque constructs a kind of organic catalogue raisonné, indexing women’s experiences of their bodies from the fifteen-hundreds to the eighteen-hundreds. Her account is assembled from sharp examples. The “supposedly simple and natural gesture” of breast-feeding, for instance, came to be ruled by a “coarse moralism” in the eighteenth century, when the act “became the primary scene of sentimental motherhood: done out of a strictly defined maternal love” rather than as paid work.

The Shampoo Effect
by Jenny Jackson ( Pamela Dorman )
Fiction
At the outset of this chatty novel, the protagonist, Caroline, who was recently ghosted by a thoughtless man, has had a story published in this magazine. In an uncharacteristically impulsive move, she decides to quit her job and write full time. Because her mother is a successful writer—and likely a narcissist—the decision is a complicated one. But soon Caroline finds herself at a seaside residency in Massachusetts, where she falls in love with a local. As she gets to know his childhood friends, whom Jackson renders vividly, further complications mount; one of the group, it emerges, is pregnant with his child. The novel is ultimately a study of the season in life when friendships are tested by growing families and by the realization of ambition.

The Savage Landscape: How We Made the Wilderness
by Cal Flyn ( Viking )
Nonfiction
What does it mean for something to be considered “wilderness” in a world saturated by human intervention? Searching for answers, Flyn travels to various remote sites—including the Transylvanian Alps; the Niassa Special Reserve, in Mozambique; and the Southern Ocean, near Antarctica—journeys that lead her to conclude that wilderness is “a negative definition, an absence.” For one thing, wild places are increasingly threatened by the trophy-hunting industry, scientific study, and corporate exploitation. But, for another, Flyn argues, wilderness is about being able to “open oneself to the immensity of all existence, all creation, all of everything.”

The Ego Trip
by Kimon de Greef ( Doubleday )
Nonfiction
De Greef’s true-crime thriller, which grew from reporting originally published in The New Yorker , explores the origins of the toad-smoking movement, and the trail of death and abuse that one psychedelic guru left in his wake.

Queen Mab
by Emily McBride ( Farrar, Straus & Giroux )
Fiction
Madeleine is a “ promising ” twenty-three-year-old graduate student who decides, to the shock of other academic women in her life, to have a baby. (“They all say congrats, by the way, and better you than them,” one colleague says.) The body horror of birth gives way to the fairy-tale horror of early motherhood, which McBride, a translator based in Barcelona, strews with literary Easter eggs from folktales and Victorian poetry. Is the baby really a baby, or has it been replaced by a changeling? Is Madeleine still herself, or has she been stolen away, too? Can her husband be trusted? The result is an agile, unsettling novel about the unwinding of a mind, set in a world of women who view motherhood as a curious affectation.

Daylight Come
by Joshua Jelly-Schapiro ( Penguin Press )
Nonfiction
This biography of Harry Belafonte, who died in 2023, paints the singer and civil-rights activist as “our first post-racial pop star.” In his music, Belafonte sought to honor his Caribbean heritage—he was born in Harlem to Jamaican parents in 1927—without being reduced to a mere exotic persona. Throughout his career, he merged his work as an entertainer with his political convictions (he refused to perform in segregated venues, for instance), a pursuit that required him to square his fame “with his anger at the society that gave it to him.” Jelly-Schapiro draws on a range of sources, including conversations with Belafonte, presenting a portrait of a formidable figure who, as Belafonte’s son puts it, “was serving two families: us and the family of Man.”

We Were Forbidden
by Jacqueline Harpman , translated from the French by Ros Schwartz ( Transit )
Fiction
In “The Ardennes Forest,” one of the three newly translated stories in “We Were Forbidden,” male and female soldiers rove aimlessly through the woods, unsure whether they’re still at war. The story’s dreamlike, surreal style permits few identifying markers; we never find out what conflict the characters have stumbled into, only that they await the activation of their “post-hypnotic orders.” “The Outcast” similarly circles feelings of entrapment, disorientation, and exile: its narrator is unkind to a hypocritical classmate at her French school in Morocco, and her teachers punish her with forty days of “ostracization,” during which no one speaks to her and she doesn’t speak to anyone. The gem of the collection is its longest story, “The Broom Closet,” an arch, light-fingered, and very funny exploration of the relationship between fantasy and fiction-making.

Dooneen
by Keith Ridgway ( New Directions )
Fiction
This strange, ambitious novel is set in a version of Dublin where cars have been banned and people enter the country by teleportation. Bartholomew Port, an Irish writer living in London, returns to his homeland to participate in a literary festival, and arrives on the eve of a populist uprising. Dublin, he observes, has become a machine “for enriching the rich” and “impoverishing the poor,” a place where “life is not as important as money.” As Port falls in with a group of conspirators preparing for the insurrection, the book takes on a hallucinatory, digressive quality, blurring the lines between life and death, reality and illusion. Ultimately, Ridgway asks what responsibility bystanders must take for the injustices around them.

The Frenchmen
by Emily Eakin ( Penguin Press )
Nonfiction
This stylish group biography of eight structuralist and post-structuralist philosophers interweaves details of its subjects’ lives with careful close readings and memoir. Eakin, an editor at the Times Book Review , aims to “re-embody” the so-called French theorists, “to recover the hidden human element beneath their often stringent antihumanism.” Her biographical approach allows her to highlight connections that a more straightforward intellectual history might not, such as the role that a chance encounter between the linguist Roman Jakobson and the anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss played in the development of the latter’s thought.

From Our Pages
Beginning Middle End
by Valeria Luiselli ( Knopf )
Fiction
After an “entangled divorce,” a woman escapes with her daughter to Catania, a port city on Sicily’s eastern coast. Upon arrival, they are met with an ominous forecast: Mt. Etna has “spewed a plume of ash and gas,” a lunar eclipse is imminent, and the Levante, a strong easterly wind, will soon blow in. Amid the ever-shifting atmosphere, mother and daughter each search for “the chance to begin, or to begin again.” The novel was excerpted in the magazine.

The Renoir Girls
by Catherine Ostler ( Atria )
Nonfiction
This sweeping biography of the daughters of a French Jewish banking dynasty—who were painted by Renoir, and counted Proust as a family friend—unfolds in parallel worlds: a glittering Paris of privilege, and a Paris where widespread poverty and political instability fuelled profound social anxiety. Ostler traces a thread of anti-Jewish hatred through both worlds, as she illustrates how the sisters’ rarefied existence was frequently marred by bursts of prejudice. In 1882, shortly after completing the girls’ portraits, for instance, Renoir declared that he was “washing my hands of the Jews.” As Ostler shows, his stated reasons were vague and irrelevant. Renoir was merely a “cork in the current” of antisemitism.

Air
by Christian Kracht , translated from the German by Daniel Bowles ( Liveright )
Fiction
Two story lines anchor this novel: one centered on a present-day designer with a Luddism-inflected aesthetic, and one that takes place in a fantastical realm where a young girl accidentally shoots a man she has mistaken for a deer. In the first plot, the designer disappears during a solar storm while working on a project in Norway. In the second, the girl and the man run from soldiers sent by a malevolent ruler. In that reality, people live on what they forage and kill; they wear shared clothes; they don’t have inventions like mirrors or—crucially—antibiotics. Though this world lacks the twenty-first-century trappings that so bothered the designer, its brutalities also suggest that nostalgia for the pre-modern is a knife that cuts both ways.

I Want You to Be Happy
by Jem Calder ( Farrar, Straus & Giroux )
Fiction
“A new person finding you interesting makes you feel new.” So reflects one of the protagonists of this intimate novel, which follows the relationship between two creative aspirants in London—a young woman working as a barista while nursing dreams of poetry, and a slightly older man who is a copywriter, but hopes to become a novelist. The two meet at a bar one night, then go home together. As Calder tracks the course of their romance, from the careful texting of its early days to reckonings with the characters’ darker elements—the copywriter, it emerges, drinks excessively—he gives the perennial human features of self-sabotage and solipsism a fresh look.

The Miraculous Season
by V. R. “Bunny” Lang ( New York Review Books )
Poetry
The American poet Violet Ranney Lang was born in 1924 and died in 1956, of Hodgkin’s lymphoma, at the age of thirty-two. She may have been cut off in her prime, but her prime is indisputably her own. Lang produced poems with a singular blend of severity and skittishness. In her tart, forbidding lines, she comes across as both quite at ease in aristocratic settings (she was a débutante born in Boston, to old money) and all too eager to smash their social rules. “The Miraculous Season,” which was first published in the U.K., in 2024, gathers some of the poetry she produced as a serious young writer, when she studied at Harvard, befriended Frank O’Hara, wrote and directed and performed in plays, and, finally, squared up to the facts of death as she had to the facts of her life—with cheerfully desperate bravado.

Glyph
by Ali Smith ( Pantheon )
Fiction
Continuing its decorated author’s project of devising a contemporary language for fiction while revisiting the past, this novel follows two sisters, Patricia and Petra, long estranged, who are haunted by stories from their childhood: one of a man who was shot during the First World War, and the other of a person who met a gruesome death in the Second. Amid the disappointments of the present—oppressive digital technology and work uncertainty—ghosts and shared recollections bring the sisters together, and closer to Patricia’s adopted daughter, Bill, who represents both the pessimism and the idealism of a younger generation. Animated by dialogue and wordplay, Smith’s novel shines with her intuition, and her ability to surprise.

Cool Machine
by Colson Whitehead ( Doubleday )
Fiction
In the gripping conclusion of his New York crime trilogy, Whitehead takes us to early nineteen-eighties Harlem, where the protagonist Ray Carney, like the entire city, seems to be on the rise. New York is recovering from near-bankruptcy, roused by the promise of Reaganomics; Carney has been named Dealer of the Month at his furniture store and plans to abandon the brutal criminality that’s plagued his family for generations—after one more heist. Hoping to help his wife start a business, he mixes with a master malefactor and is plunged back into the city’s felonious landscape. His devotion to his spouse, allegiance to a dangerous old accomplice, and grief over the murder of his cousin threaten an existence he has spent years building. Whitehead, a winner of two Pulitzer Prizes, gives the Harlem Trilogy a finale that pays haunting homage to the imperfect city where he and his characters are perpetually reinvented.

Élisabeth
by Éric Rohmer , translated from the French by Aaron Kerner ( McNally Editions )
Fiction
Constructed as a set of ruses and evasions, “Élisabeth” was the only novel that the great French New Wave filmmaker Rohmer ever wrote. Completed in the summer of 1944, amid battles for the liberation of Paris from Nazi occupiers, the book’s narrative begins in 1939, with characters anticipating the end of summer and a return to business as usual in the fall, unaware of what is to come. “Élisabeth” depicts a social world that manages to survive cataclysm: even during the Occupation, people go to college, hold jobs, take vacations, flirt, marry, separate, and write. Its central character, Michel, is an engineer in his early twenties who is having doubts about his engagement to a woman named Irène, a widow a few years older than he. As Rohmer pursues this through line, he flits from character to character, location to location, assembling a book that is ultimately an exemplary modernist novel.

The Cruelty of Nice Folks
by Justin Ellis ( Harper )
Nonfiction
Minneapolis has long been a stronghold of progressivism: slavery was banned there upon Minnesota’s statehood, and it was an early adopter of public housing. But, as Ellis demonstrates in this survey of the city’s racial history, liberal policy achievements tend to obscure more insidious forms of exclusion. A Minneapolis native, Ellis returns to his home after the murder of George Floyd. His resulting exploration tracks the ways in which Black residents were effectively segregated, through racial covenants and redlining, and overpoliced. Though Ellis’s long view of the city is tinged with cynicism, its response to last winter’s ICE invasion creates, he contends, an opening for hope.

Death of the Soccer God
by Dimitry Elias Léger ( MCD x FSG )
Fiction
This stylish historical picaresque examines Haitian identity and history by recounting the “brief, wondrous life” of a fictional athlete, Gilbert Chevalier. Born to a wealthy family in Port-au-Prince, the young Chevalier has a prodigious talent for soccer. When he’s dispatched to Columbia University for college, he rooms with Miles Davis, consorts with John Coltrane, and is recruited to play for the United States in the 1950 World Cup, in Brazil. There he meets a nine-year-old Pelé and leads the American team to a stunning upset of England. Returning to Haiti after playing professional football in Europe, Chevalier runs afoul of President François Duvalier—an incident with dangerous consequences.

From Our Pages
They Stole a City
by Lauren Collins ( Penguin Press )
Nonfiction
In this gripping narrative, part history and part reportage, Collins, a staff writer, returns to her home town of Wilmington, North Carolina, to explore a chapter in the city’s history that was long overlooked or actively suppressed: in November, 1898, a mob of white supremacists rampaged through the streets, killing Black people and seizing the city government in what is thought to be the only successful coup d’état on American soil. The book, which was excerpted in The New Yorker , describes how the violence reverberated through generations of Wilmington families, shaping lives in ways that official histories failed to acknowledge. The racist takeover of the city happened more than a century ago, yet its lessons are urgent as ever, Collins writes: “There is no more explicit example of the vulnerability of American democracy, and of the magnitude of the task of repairing it once it is breached.”

Spawning Season
by Joseph Osmundson ( Bloomsbury )
Nonfiction
Anchored by a poignant account of his efforts to become a father, this memoir, by a microbiologist, is also a wide-ranging meditation on what it means to be biologically “fit” in Western society today. Though the barriers to parenthood which Osmundson encounters don’t exist for all of us (he’s queer; he’s male; he’s not able to afford surrogacy or adoption), his emotional journey will be instantly recognizable to anyone whose dreams of having a child have been dashed or deferred. Some of that arc is grappling with various reasons not to have a child, including climate change. A secondary narrative, following salmon on their journey to reproduce in warming waters, proves surprisingly apposite, partly thanks to Osmundson’s expertise on the subject, and partly because it underscores what is uniquely human about his dilemma: that, for us, a universal instinct can also be a question.

The Perfect Moment
by Isaac Butler ( Bloomsbury )
Nonfiction
In this lively history, Butler revisits the American culture wars that started in the late nineteen-eighties, chronicling how cöordinated conservative campaigns transformed obscure disputes over federal museum grants into defining battles for the soul of the Republican Party. Along the way, indelible scenes of senators ripping exhibition catalogues and inviting “women and children” to leave the Senate chamber before brandishing Robert Mapplethorpe’s photographs lend the political history novelistic propulsion. The culture wars, Butler suggests, are less a closed chapter than a continuing conflict: if “the culture wars of the late twentieth century were the World War I of American arts and letters,” he writes, “we have now entered World War II.”

Nebraska
by Monica Datta ( Astra )
Fiction
This ambitious novel springs from a moment of apparent inhuman cruelty: a mother, Anna Chatterjee, kills her disabled son, pushing his wheelchair in front of an oncoming train. The murder and its fraught causes are recounted by a Bengali analyst, who is himself interpreting them from the records of a different analyst with connections to Chatterjee’s two living children. When these two children, along with Chatterjee’s husband, attempt to pick her up at the end of her prison sentence, they find she is already gone. Datta explores the impact of enormous colonial forces on the unconscious of a single individual, her narrative shifting between time lines and continents in a performance that is both dizzying and energizing.

Axe in Blossom
by Franz Wright ( Knopf )
Poetry
Wright, who died in 2015, composed these poems while suffering from lung cancer, recording many of them in scribbles around his apartment in Waltham, Massachusetts. And yet his condition is never an occasion for self-pity; his lines glow, instead, with the light of honesty and self-deprecation. He remarks on his “odd-sounding croak that was once a good voice”; at another point, spotting his reflection in a bus, he writes, “I looked like a suicide / returning an overdue book to the library.” Wright has a gift for tender, wisecracking moments, and he renders them with extraordinary sensory detail, whether he’s observing something as close as a fly or as distant as the stars.

Muskism
by Quinn Slobodian Ben Tarnoff ( Harper )

Dickson writes with a refreshing absence of self-pity, and with empathy even for mothers whose practices and preferences differ vastly from her own.

Bernie for Burlington
by Dan Chiasson ( Knopf )
Nonfiction
In 1971, Bernie Sanders moved to Burlington and made his first run for the U.S. Senate, winning 2.2 per cent of the vote. That same year, blocks away from Sanders’s apartment, Dan Chiasson was born. Chiasson, a poet, a longtime contributor to this magazine, and the chair of the English department at Wellesley, had a front-row seat to Sanders’s rise, and his revelatory new book is nearly as much a memoir of its author as it is a biography of its subject and, not least, a history of the Green Mountain State. Sanders’s attraction to Vermont can be traced back to a moment when he, as a young man, came across a brochure from a Vermont travel bureau. “It is no small irony,” Chiasson writes, “that hill farms marketed to well-heeled city people piqued the interest of a thirteen-year-old Brooklyn Jew and future socialist who would arguably do more to impact Vermont’s traditional culture than anyone in the state’s history.”

Everything Is Photograph
by Patricia Albers ( Other Press )
Nonfiction
This biography tracks the triumphs and the travails of the twentieth-century Hungarian photographer André Kertész. Kertész’s compositions are notably strange—often off center and taken from high angles, they appear like nervous half glances at scenes of pedestrian shuffle—and many are reproduced here, enriched by thorough commentary by Albers. Her exploration of Kertész’s time as an infantryman in the First World War is especially illuminating, as she documents the curiously “flirtatious tender touch” with which he photographed his surroundings. This kind of artistic contradiction becomes a theme, as Albers unfurls details about Kertész’s romantic life, his move to America, and his later fame.

This Is Where the Serpent Lives
by Daniyal Mueenuddin ( Knopf )
Fiction
Mueenuddin’s powerfully absorbing novel charts the intricate interplay between landowners and their servants in a feudal Pakistan. Among other narratives, he traces the trajectory of one man, Bayazid—orphaned, or abandoned, as a young child in the years after Partition—who comes to accept that, though he may have left his lowly job at a tandoori stall behind, he will never rise beyond his role as a chauffeur to a wealthy family. Years later, Saqib, a similarly ambitious young man, whom Bayazid has championed, dreams of acquiring some of the riches of his employers but instead discovers that his deviously brilliant scheming could destroy him.
